case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may order DHS to process or facilitate access to asylum for noncitizens at or near ports of entry when DHS uses (or could use) “metering” or similar practices to turn people back or delay their presentation for inspection, and whether such claims are barred by jurisdiction-stripping provisions or foreclosed by Supreme Court precedent.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act provisions governing inspection and asylum at ports of entry (principally 8 U.S.C. § 1225 (inspection/applicants for admission; expedited removal; credible-fear/asylum screening) and 8 U.S.C. § 1158 (right to apply for asylum)), and related limits on judicial review (commonly 8 U.S.C. § 1252); Article III mootness justiciability doctrines are also implicated by the rescission of metering but ongoing classwide/individual injunctive relief.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (DHS/Secretary Noem) argue that the Ninth Circuit improperly allowed broad programmatic challenges to border-management practices like metering and that the requested relief effectively forces the Executive to admit or process individuals contrary to statutory structure, discretion, and jurisdictional limits. They contend (1) the relevant INA provisions do not impose the kind of judicially enforceable, nondiscretionary duty respondents claim (especially regarding who is considered “in the United States” and the mechanics/timing of inspection at a port of entry), (2) respondents’ suit is barred or constrained by INA jurisdiction-stripping and channeling provisions (including limits on review of removal-related decisions and expedited-removal screening), and (3) Supreme Court precedent (including decisions addressing habeas limits and the scope of judicial intervention in immigration enforcement) supports restricting this kind of injunctive relief. Petitioners also maintain the case remains justiciable despite policy changes because the district court’s declaration and injunction continue to have operative effect for the class and at least one named plaintiff.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Al Otro Lado and affected asylum seekers) argue that the INA imposes mandatory duties at ports of entry: when a person presents at a port of entry and seeks asylum, DHS must inspect/process them under § 1225 and must allow them to apply for asylum under § 1158, rather than preventing access through “metering” or pushbacks that keep them on the Mexico side of the line. They emphasize statutory text and history (including pre-IIRIRA practice) to argue that asylum/inspection obligations attach based on arrival/presentation at a port of entry, not only after physical entry beyond the border line. They contend jurisdiction-stripping provisions do not bar their claims because they challenge systemic obstruction of statutory access to asylum and inspection (ultra vires/unlawful conduct), not individualized discretionary judgments or final orders of removal. They further argue key Supreme Court cases cited by the government—such as Sale and Thuraissigiam—are inapposite because they concern different statutory frameworks and/or habeas review of expedited-removal determinations after entry, not government practices that prevent people from reaching the inspection and asylum-processing regime in the first place. They also suggest that deciding legality in the absence of an active policy risks an advisory opinion, while acknowledging ongoing injunctive effects may defeat mootness.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, 601 U.S. 1 (2023) (mootness principles referenced in oral argument excerpts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan make the strongest point that “metering” can operate as a pre-process blockade that may evade § 1252(b)(9) and is not squarely resolved by Thuraissigiam. But even taking that characterization as given, Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas are right that § 1252(f)(1), as construed in Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, is a hard remedial limit: lower courts lack authority to enter classwide, programmatic relief that effectively dictates how DHS must run § 1225’s inspection regime at ports, which is what the judgment below does in practical operation. Sotomayor’s proposal to salvage the case through declaratory relief does not solve the institutional problem here because, in this posture, the declaration would function as operational supervision and thus still “restrain the operation” of Part IV. A minimalist resolution—vacating or reversing on § 1252(f)(1) grounds, especially given the policy’s rescission—respects Congress’s remedial choices while leaving room for genuinely individualized relief where the INA permits it.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point—that metering is an ultra vires, “pre-process” blockade outside the INA’s channeling provisions—does not answer the separate and dispositive text of § 1252(f)(1), which withdraws lower-court “jurisdiction or authority” to grant relief that would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV. As Justice Gorsuch notes, Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez reads § 1252(f)(1) as a hard remedial bar against programmatic injunctions, and the order here functionally directs how DHS must conduct § 1225 inspections at ports of entry, thereby restraining its operation. Even if Article III permits declaring what the law is, the only meaningful relief sought here is operational compulsion on a systemwide basis, and § 1252(f)(1)’s narrow exception for “an individual alien” cannot be expanded to cover a classwide decree. I therefore remain with the Chief Justice and others that we should reverse or vacate on remedial-authority grounds without reaching broader merits questions about §§ 1158/1225.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor are right to press that § 1158(a)(1)’s parenthetical (“whether or not at a designated port of arrival”) can naturally encompass those who present at a port and that “metering” might functionally frustrate Congress’s front-end scheme. But even accepting that merits framing, Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Thomas’s point is dispositive here: § 1252(f)(1), as construed in Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, withdraws lower-court authority to enter classwide, programmatic injunctions that “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, and the order below effectively dictates how DHS must run § 1225 processing at ports. Justice Sotomayor’s ultra vires characterization does not cure the remedial defect, because the relief still operates as systemwide operational supervision rather than the individualized relief Congress allowed, and Thuraissigiam reinforces the need to respect the INA’s remedial limits in this border-processing context. I therefore remain with the Petitioner to reverse or vacate on § 1252(f)(1) grounds without broad merits pronouncements.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Gorsuch’s point that § 1252(f)(1), especially after Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, bars lower courts from issuing classwide, programmatic injunctions that effectively supervise DHS’s ongoing operation of § 1225 at ports. But that remedial limit should not be transformed—via labels like “jurisdiction or authority”—into a merits-jurisdiction blackout for threshold ultra vires obstruction claims alleging DHS prevents people from ever reaching Congress’s mandatory inspection/credible-fear machinery in §§ 1225(a)(1), (b) and the asylum entitlement in § 1158(a)(1) (including its “whether or not at a designated port of arrival” parenthetical). Justice Thomas is right that the injunction below likely overreaches, yet the appropriate response is to narrow relief (declaratory and genuinely individualized remedies) rather than to treat § 1252(f)(1) as insulating systemic pre-process shutouts from judicial correction. On my pragmatic approach, we must avoid an interpretation that allows the Executive to nullify statutory protections for vulnerable asylum seekers simply by controlling access to the process Congress mandated.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and the Chief’s strongest point is that § 1252(f)(1), as read in Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, squarely forbids lower courts from issuing classwide, forward-looking injunctions that effectively manage DHS’s portwide administration of § 1225—and I agree the injunction as crafted cannot stand. But that remedial bar does not, textually, extinguish judicial power to decide whether DHS is acting ultra vires by preventing noncitizens from ever reaching the mandatory inspection/credible-fear machinery in §§ 1225(a)(1)–(b) and the asylum-application entitlement in § 1158(a)(1), before any expedited-removal “determination” exists to trigger the INA’s tight review channels. Justice Alito’s “arrives in” territorial-line reading is plausible, yet it sits uneasily with § 1158(a)(1)’s parenthetical (“whether or not at a designated port of arrival”) and the statute’s integrated port-of-entry inspection scheme, making it at least as natural to treat presentation at a port as triggering statutory duties. The pragmatic, text-faithful middle course is therefore to recognize potential liability (and permit individualized or genuinely non-supervisory declaratory relief) while narrowing or vacating the programmatic injunction under § 1252(f)(1), rather than treating that provision as functional immunity for pre-process shutouts.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: that “metering” can be a pre-process obstruction that prevents anyone from ever entering the § 1225 inspection/credible-fear machinery, so channeling provisions may not neatly apply. But even accepting that framing, § 1252(f)(1) independently withdraws lower-court “jurisdiction or authority” to award the very sort of classwide, forward-looking decree entered here, and Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez (as Justice Thomas emphasizes) reads that text as a firm remedies bar against programmatic injunctions that manage DHS’s administration of Part IV. Justice Kagan is right that Article III adjudicatory power is not extinguished, yet the requested relief—port-wide operational commands—still “enjoin[s] or restrain[s] the operation” of § 1225 in the sense Congress prohibited. Consistent with the Chief’s minimalist approach, I would reverse or vacate on remedial limits without broad merits pronouncements, leaving only whatever genuinely individualized relief the statute allows.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest merits point: metering can operate as a pre-process barrier that prevents noncitizens from ever reaching Congress’s mandatory inspection/credible-fear machinery, and they plausibly argue § 1252(b)(9) shouldn’t be stretched to choke off that kind of ultra vires claim. But even accepting that framing, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch that § 1252(f)(1)—as construed in Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez—withdraws lower-court authority to enter classwide, programmatic relief that effectively dictates port-of-entry processing and thus “enjoin[s] or restrain[s] the operation” of § 1225. The respondents’ proposed pivot to declaratory relief does not, in this posture, cure the problem because the judgment below functions as ongoing operational supervision rather than case-specific adjudication within Congress’s narrow exception. Under a precedent- and institution-focused approach, the narrow and proper disposition is to reverse or vacate on remedial-authority grounds without opining broadly on the scope of any affirmative access duty under §§ 1158/1225.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the strongest point that “metering” can operate as a pre-process blockade, potentially preventing noncitizens from ever reaching Congress’s inspection and credible-fear framework, and that Thuraissigiam does not squarely address that posture. But even accepting their characterization, § 1252(f)(1)’s text—withdrawal of lower-court “jurisdiction or authority” to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV—still forecloses the programmatic, port-wide injunction entered here, and Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez (as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas emphasize) reads that bar as a hard remedial limit on classwide, forward-looking relief. Justice Sotomayor’s ultra vires framing may bear on whether any legal duty exists, but it does not answer the distinct remedial question: the order below functionally dictates how DHS must administer § 1225 at ports, which is exactly the sort of operational supervision Congress prohibited. On an originalist and textualist reading, the proper disposition is to reverse or vacate on remedial-authority grounds, leaving open whatever individualized relief Congress has permitted without opining broadly on the scope of any affirmative access obligation under § 1158(a)(1).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch are right that § 1252(f)(1), especially after Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez, is a substantial remedial constraint and likely forecloses the classwide, programmatic injunction entered here. But I am not persuaded by Justice Thomas’s and Justice Alito’s broader move from that remedial bar to functional immunity for pre-process obstruction: Aleman Gonzalez limits the availability of injunctions; it does not eliminate Article III power to adjudicate whether DHS is acting ultra vires in a way that prevents any § 1225 “inspection” or § 1225(b) credible-fear steps from ever occurring (and thus prevents entry into § 1252(e)’s narrow review channel). On the merits, Justice Alito’s “arrives in” versus “arrives at” distinction is textually plausible, yet it is hard to reconcile with § 1158(a)(1)’s parenthetical (“whether or not at a designated port of arrival”) and the statute’s overall design that makes inspection and referral mandatory once an applicant presents for processing. The pragmatic, procedurally fair course is to recognize that the injunction as framed exceeds § 1252(f)(1) while preserving the judiciary’s role to declare illegality and permit genuinely individualized relief where Congress allows it, rather than treating § 1252(f)(1) as a wholesale jurisdiction-stripping device for threshold shutouts.

John Roberts.reasoning: This suit seeks broad injunctive relief that would effectively supervise DHS’s operation of the inspection and expedited-removal scheme at ports of entry, a domain Congress tightly regulated in 8 U.S.C. § 1225 and substantially insulated from equitable intervention through 8 U.S.C. § 1252’s channeling and remedial limits. Even assuming some statutory obligations exist under § 1158 and § 1225, the requested classwide, programmatic orders compelling processing and access would "interfere with" the Executive’s administration of § 1225 in a manner Congress restricted, and the Court should avoid an expansive merits holding given the rescinded policy and serious advisory-opinion/mootness concerns flagged at argument. Narrowly resolving on jurisdiction/remedy grounds best preserves institutional legitimacy and respects Congress’s allocation of immigration-enforcement discretion, while leaving room for individualized, properly channeled review where Congress has authorized it. Thuraissigiam reinforces that courts should not expand judicial review beyond what § 1252 permits in the expedited-removal/asylum-screening context, and that background counsels against district-court injunctions that effectively compel admission or processing outside the statute’s review scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s text channels and limits judicial interference with the Executive’s administration of inspection and expedited-removal provisions, and respondents’ requested classwide injunction effectively compels how DHS must "operate" §§ 1225 and related provisions at the border. Section 1252(f)(1) by its terms bars lower courts from enjoining or restraining the operation of the covered statutory scheme (8 U.S.C. §§ 1221–1232), and an order requiring DHS to process or facilitate access at or near ports of entry is precisely the sort of programmatic, systemwide relief Congress foreclosed. Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez confirms that § 1252(f)(1) means what it says and precludes such broad injunctive relief, and any attempt to recharacterize the injunction as anchored in § 1158 cannot evade the practical effect of restraining § 1225’s operation. Consistent with Thuraissigiam, the Court should not expand federal-court review beyond what Congress provided in § 1252, particularly in matters at the border where Congress has assigned primary responsibility to the political branches.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1) limits the “right to apply for asylum” to an alien who is “physically present in the United States” or who “arrives in the United States,” and it is not clear that a person kept on the Mexico side by “metering” has satisfied that statutory condition; federal courts should not rewrite “arrives in” into “arrives at.” Even if §§ 1225 and 1158 impose certain mandatory steps once an applicant is presented for inspection, ordering DHS to affirmatively facilitate entry or access to ports would entail programmatic injunctive control over border operations that Congress sought to preclude through 8 U.S.C. § 1252’s channeling and jurisdiction-limiting scheme, particularly § 1252(a)(2)(A)’s restrictions on review of expedited-removal-related policies and implementation. Our decisions caution against expanding judicial review and remedies in this area beyond what the INA expressly permits; DHS v. Thuraissigiam underscores Congress’s broad authority to restrict judicial intervention in the expedited-removal/asylum screening framework and counsels against the kind of broad, systemwide relief entered here. Practical consequences also favor deference to the Executive’s border-management judgments rather than judicially mandated processing protocols that could functionally compel admission.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Sections 1225 and 1158 impose mandatory, front-end obligations: when a noncitizen presents at a port of entry and indicates a fear or intent to seek asylum, DHS must inspect and, if fear is expressed, provide the screening mechanisms Congress prescribed; “metering” practices that block or delay presentation functionally nullify those statutory commands. The jurisdiction-channeling provisions in § 1252(a)(2) and (b)(9) should not be read to bar an ultra vires/systemic claim that DHS is preventing access to the inspection/asylum regime before any removal proceeding begins, especially where the suit does not seek review of an expedited-removal determination or a final order. Thuraissigiam is not controlling because it addressed the constitutionality of limiting habeas review after an expedited-removal process had occurred, not whether courts may remedy government action that prevents people from reaching the process at all. While § 1252(f)(1) as construed in Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez sharply limits classwide injunctions that “enjoin or restrain the operation” of covered provisions like § 1225, it does not eliminate Article III jurisdiction to adjudicate legality and affords room for declaratory relief and, at minimum, individualized relief for named plaintiffs to ensure access to the statutory scheme.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1158(a)(1) provides that "[a]ny alien who is physically present in the United States or who arrives in the United States (whether or not at a designated port of arrival)" may apply for asylum, and the most natural reading of "arrives" at a port of entry encompasses noncitizens who present themselves for inspection rather than only those who have crossed an invisible territorial line. Coupled with § 1225(a)(1)–(b)’s mandatory inspection and credible-fear screening scheme for "applicants for admission" and "arriving" noncitizens, systemic “metering” that prevents presentation for inspection plausibly circumvents Congress’s processing mandates, making narrowly tailored injunctive relief workable and textually grounded. The principal jurisdictional limits the Government invokes—especially § 1252(e) (limiting review of expedited-removal determinations) and § 1252(f)(1) (restricting classwide injunctions to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of the relevant provisions)—do not clearly bar a suit alleging ultra vires obstruction of access to the statutory regime before any expedited-removal decision occurs, though § 1252(f)(1) may require narrowing remedies to individuals rather than broad programmatic commands. Neither Sale nor Thuraissigiam forecloses this claim because they addressed different contexts (extraterritorial interdiction and habeas limits after expedited-removal proceedings, respectively), not a challenge to practices that prevent entry into § 1225’s inspection/asylum-processing framework in the first place.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The relief respondents seek runs headlong into Congress’s unmistakable limit on lower-court injunctions in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1), which withdraws “jurisdiction or authority” to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV (including § 1225) except as applied to “an individual alien against whom” proceedings have been initiated; under Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, § 1252(f)(1) is a remedies bar, and Garland v. Aleman Gonzalez confirms it forecloses classwide injunctive orders that effectively supervise the operation of these provisions. Even if §§ 1158 and 1225 impose mandatory duties in some settings, separation-of-powers principles caution against programmatic, forward-looking injunctions that dictate how the Executive must manage access to ports of entry, especially where the challenged “metering” policy has been rescinded and Article III concerns press against issuing advisory pronouncements about hypothetical future practices. At most, any judicial relief must be limited to truly individualized, concrete claims within the narrow exception Congress provided, not classwide directives reengineering border processing.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The requested relief is a classic programmatic injunction compelling how DHS must manage inspection and access to asylum at the border, and the INA’s channeling and review-limiting provisions—especially 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9) and the narrow review scheme in § 1252(e) tied to expedited removal—counsel strongly against district-court supervision of such border-wide operational policies. The statutory text in 8 U.S.C. §§ 1158(a)(1) and 1225 speaks in terms of noncitizens who are “in the United States” or “applicants for admission,” and it is at least doubtful that it creates a judicially enforceable, nondiscretionary duty to process persons who have not been permitted to present for inspection at the port-of-entry line; in that setting, judicial restraint and practical workability caution against courts ordering affirmative facilitation at or near the border. Thuraissigiam reinforces that Congress may tightly limit judicial review in this domain and that courts should be reluctant to expand remedies beyond the review scheme Congress prescribed, particularly where the effect would be to mandate processing or entry. Given the rescission of metering and the continuing injunction’s breadth, the proper course is to reverse and limit lower-court remedial power consistent with § 1252’s structure and the Court’s immigration precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of § 1158(a)(1) extends the ability to apply for asylum to a noncitizen who is “physically present in the United States” or who “arrives in the United States (whether or not at a designated port of arrival),” and the most natural reading of “in” denotes territorial presence rather than being held outside the line by DHS; § 1225 likewise presupposes an “applicant for admission” presented “for inspection” within the inspection regime rather than a judicially enforceable obligation to bring persons on the Mexico side into that regime. Even assuming some access duty exists, § 1252’s channeling and jurisdiction-limiting provisions—especially § 1252(b)(9) (consolidating review of “all questions of law and fact” arising from removal-related actions) and § 1252(f)(1) (restricting classwide injunctions that “enjoin or restrain the operation” of the relevant INA provisions)—counsel strongly against programmatic, classwide injunctive relief compelling DHS to process entrants at or near ports of entry. Our precedent warns against expanding judicial review in this area beyond what Congress has specified; in Thuraissigiam we emphasized Congress’s broad control over the remedial and review structure for expedited-removal/asylum screening, and that logic supports refusing to use equitable/APA-style relief to circumvent the statutory review scheme. Given the rescission of metering but continuing operative injunction and declaration, the case is not moot, but the appropriate disposition is to vacate or narrow relief because the lower courts exceeded their authority under the INA’s text and review-limiting framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Sections 1158(a)(1) and 1225(a)(1) use mandatory language that, on respondents’ theory, attaches when a noncitizen presents at a port of entry and seeks protection, and metering/pushbacks that prevent access to inspection plausibly amount to ultra vires obstruction of those nondiscretionary statutory duties rather than a challenge to individualized removal decisions. The jurisdiction-channeling provisions in § 1252 are strongest when plaintiffs seek review of expedited-removal determinations or specific discretionary judgments, but respondents’ claim targets a systemic practice that keeps people from entering the § 1225/credible-fear regime at all, making Thuraissigiam (habeas limits after an expedited-removal determination) and Sale (extraterritorial interdiction) materially distinguishable. On justiciability, rescission of the challenged policy does not necessarily moot the case while a classwide declaration and ongoing injunction continue to operate; the Court can address the live controversy over the continuing force/scope of that relief under modern mootness principles reflected in Acheson Hotels and related voluntary-cessation doctrine rather than issuing an advisory opinion. Given the practical consequences and procedural fairness concerns at the border, I would affirm the availability of narrowly tailored relief requiring DHS to provide access to the statutory inspection/asylum process when individuals present at ports of entry, while policing overbroad classwide injunctions under § 1252(f)(1).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether DHS may implement or retain a “metering” policy that turns away or delays would-be asylum seekers at (or just outside) ports of entry without triggering the Immigration and Nationality Act’s inspection and asylum-processing duties, and whether federal courts can enjoin that practice on a classwide basis.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), principally 8 U.S.C. § 1225 (inspection and processing of applicants for admission, including individuals who present at a port of entry), along with related asylum provisions (e.g., 8 U.S.C. § 1158) and threshold Article III justiciability limits (mootness/advisory opinion concerns).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The government argues that the INA’s inspection/asylum-processing mandates are triggered only when a noncitizen is physically “in the United States” at a port of entry (not merely “at” the border line or approaching it), leaving DHS discretion to control throughput and queueing at ports (i.e., metering) as a border-management measure. Petitioners also press procedural/justiciability limits: they suggest the case risks becoming effectively advisory because the challenged policy has been rescinded and there are no concrete plans to reinstate it, and they contest the breadth/continuing effect of injunctive relief and the propriety of classwide remedies compelling entry or processing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend that the INA requires DHS to inspect and process individuals who present themselves for admission and express fear at ports of entry, and that “metering” unlawfully evades those mandatory duties by stopping people at or near the port (including just across the line) to prevent statutory protections from attaching. They argue Congress designed § 1225 and asylum statutes to apply upon presentation at ports and that allowing DHS to redefine the trigger point would permit circumvention (including pushing enforcement further into Mexico) and ultra vires conduct. Respondents also maintain the case remains live because the judgment has continuing classwide and individual effects (including an order to facilitate entry for a named plaintiff), and that judicial relief is appropriate to prevent repetition and to remedy ongoing consequences of the challenged practice.
key_precedents: Sale v. Haitian Centers Council, Inc., 509 U.S. 155 (1993)
Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, 601 U.S. 1 (2023) (mootness/standing context referenced in oral argument)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that the existing declaration/facilitation order creates continuing legal consequences and that a “game of inches” could invite evasion, but that actually reinforces my institutional concern: it is improper to leave an unreviewable, forward-looking merits judgment in place after the challenged metering policy has been rescinded, especially where the only meaningful relief now is modification or vacatur of the decree rather than an abstract construction of § 1225’s territorial trigger. Acheson Hotels, as Justice Kagan reads it, focuses on whether a court can still grant effective relief; here the effective relief is remedial—vacating or narrowing the classwide and supervisory components—so we can resolve the case on justiciability/remedy grounds without reaching the statutory merits on this attenuated record. Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) point further supports a narrow disposition: Congress sharply limited lower-court authority to issue classwide injunctive relief restraining Part IV’s operation, making it unnecessary and unwise to decide the extraterritorial reach question to clean up an overbroad decree. I therefore remain with Petitioner: the appropriate course is to reverse/vacate or remand to tailor relief consistent with Article III and § 1252(f)(1), not to announce a broad merits rule aimed at deterring hypothetical future loopholes.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “loophole/game of inches” argument is the strongest merits push, but it asks us to replace § 1225(a)(1)’s territorial trigger (“present in the United States” or “arriving in the United States”) with a functional-control test untethered to the statute’s text; administrability concerns cannot justify rewriting Congress’s chosen line. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on § 1158(a)(1) (“at a land border or port of entry”) does not supply the clear statement necessary to apply § 1225(b)’s inspection/credible-fear machinery extraterritorially, and Sale supports treating physical presence outside U.S. territory as legally significant absent explicit congressional direction. Chief Justice Roberts’s mootness/vacatur point reinforces that, given rescission and an attenuated record, we should avoid a sweeping merits construction; at minimum, Justice Alito is correct that § 1252(f)(1) forecloses the classwide, programmatic injunction here. Nothing raised undermines my textual conclusion that respondents’ threshold-expansion theory lacks a statutory anchor and that the lower court’s relief cannot stand.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “game of inches/loophole” argument is the strongest merits point, but it ultimately asks us to treat functional control on the Mexico side as statutory “presence in the United States,” which is an atextual move and effectively an extraterritorial application of § 1225(a)(1) without a clear statement. Section 1158(a)(1)’s reference to those “at a land border or port of entry,” as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, does not rewrite § 1225’s territorially phrased trigger or supply the missing procedural machinery for mandatory inspection/credible-fear processing outside the United States. On remedy, even accepting Justice Jackson’s view that some effective relief remains, § 1252(f)(1) still forecloses the sort of classwide, programmatic injunction and declaration that “enjoin[s] or restrain[s] the operation” of Part IV, and Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Comm. supports reading that bar broadly enough to require vacatur/narrowing here. Chief Justice Roberts’s Munsingwear concerns further counsel against endorsing respondents’ expansive merits theory on a rescinded policy and an attenuated record, pointing instead to limiting the continuing decree rather than affirming it.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Munsingwear/mootness framing is the strongest push, but it misconceives the posture: as Justice Kagan notes, the Government remains bound by operative relief (a classwide declaration and at least one facilitation order), so this dispute has not “evaporated,” and under Acheson Hotels effective relief still exists in the form of modification or enforcement rather than an advisory pronouncement. Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) point is real, yet it is a remedial limiter—not a merits eraser—and it supports narrowing any injunction rather than vacating merits determinations where the challenged conduct plausibly functioned as an ultra vires end-run around §§ 1225/1158. I am not persuaded by Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s territorial-trigger reading because it treats the port-of-entry/border language in § 1158(a)(1) as surplus and invites the manipulable “game of inches” loophole Justice Kagan identifies, undermining Congress’s mandatory screening scheme. Sale does not compel that extraterritorial result here; it addressed high-seas interdiction and does not authorize DHS to nullify statutory processing duties at the controlled threshold by keeping applicants a few feet outside the line.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Munsingwear/vacatur framing is the strongest push: if the case were truly moot, we should not leave a forward-looking judgment in place without merits review. But as Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson emphasize, operative relief still binds the Government (at least a named-plaintiff facilitation order and a classwide declaration), so under Acheson Hotels the dispute is not moot because a court can still grant meaningful relief by narrowing, modifying, or dissolving those constraints. On the merits, I remain unpersuaded by Justices Barrett and Gorsuch that § 1225’s “present/arriving” language turns on a manipulable, inches-based territorial trigger, especially given § 1158(a)(1)’s express coverage of those “at a land border or port of entry” and the INA’s coherence concerns; the better reading treats controlled presentation at the threshold as sufficient for the statutory processing duties. Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) argument is a serious remedial constraint, but it supports tailoring classwide relief—not declaring mootness or adopting an interpretation that allows the Executive to nullify Congress’s screening framework by moving the functional line.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “loophole/game of inches” argument is the best merits point for respondents, but it asks us to replace Congress’s territorial trigger—an alien “present in the United States” in § 1225(a)(1)—with a functional-control test untethered to the enacted text; under a textualist/originalist approach, administrability concerns cannot justify extending § 1225(b)’s inspection/credible-fear machinery to individuals on foreign soil absent a clear statement. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on § 1158(a)(1) (“at a land border or port of entry”) shows Congress knew how to speak to border situations, yet it does not supply the missing hook to apply § 1225 extraterritorially, and Sale (as Justice Thomas notes) cautions against assuming such duties outside the line without clear authorization. Chief Justice Roberts’s mootness/vacatur framing and Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) point provide a narrow, institutionally sound path to relief—at least vacatur or reversal/narrowing of the classwide, programmatic decree—without issuing an expansive merits holding on a rescinded policy. Nothing I have heard undermines the core textual point that “in the United States” cannot be judicially rewritten to mean “within U.S. officers’ physical control just across the border.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “loophole/game of inches” argument is the strongest on the other side, but under a precedent- and text-respecting approach we should not adopt a functional-control test that effectively extends § 1225’s territorial triggers beyond “present in the United States” on this record; if Congress wants duties to attach extraterritorially, it can say so. Chief Justice Roberts is right that rescission plus the attenuated forward-looking posture makes this a poor vehicle for a broad merits pronouncement; Acheson Hotels focuses on whether relief remains, and here the most institutionally appropriate relief is to vacate or materially narrow ongoing decrees rather than decide an abstract statutory-trigger question. Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) point independently supports reversal at least as to the classwide injunction because Congress sharply limited lower courts’ ability to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of these provisions, making a sweeping programmatic decree improper even if some merits dispute persists. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about continuing legal consequences strengthens, rather than weakens, the case for Munsingwear-style vacatur/narrowing instead of affirming an expansive merits holding.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “game of inches/loophole” concern is the strongest merits argument, but under a textualist approach it cannot justify treating individuals kept on the Mexico side as "present in the United States" for § 1225(a)(1); that would effectively extend a territorially triggered inspection regime extraterritorially without a clear statement. Justice Sotomayor is right that § 1158(a)(1) covers those "at a land border or port of entry," but that asylum-eligibility clause does not itself supply § 1225(b) credible-fear/processing machinery for persons not yet within U.S. territory, and reading it to override § 1225’s territorial language collapses distinct statutory triggers. On justiciability and remedy, the Chief Justice’s point that rescission plus continuing forward-looking decrees raises Munsingwear/Article III concerns reinforces resolving this case by vacating or narrowing operative relief rather than issuing a broad statutory construction on an attenuated, superseded record. Finally, Justice Alito’s § 1252(f)(1) argument provides an independent basis to reverse at least the classwide, programmatic relief, making respondents’ expansive merits theory unnecessary here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Munsingwear/mootness proposal is the most serious objection, but it proves the opposite of mootness: the Government remains concretely bound by an operative classwide declaration/injunction and a named-plaintiff facilitation order, so there is still effective relief we can grant—modification, narrowing, or dissolution—under Acheson Hotels’ focus on live remedial consequences. Justice Alito is right that § 1252(f)(1) sharply constrains classwide injunctive relief that would “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV, and I would tailor the decree accordingly rather than endorse ongoing programmatic supervision. But Justice Thomas’s territorial-trigger reading, pressed as a merits off-ramp, is too vulnerable to the manipulable “game of inches” Justice Kagan describes and does not square with § 1158(a)(1)’s express coverage of those “at a land border or port of entry,” especially where U.S. officers themselves prevent formal crossing while exercising control at the threshold. On this posture, the better course is to reach the merits only as needed to confirm illegality and then conform the remedy to § 1252(f)(1), not to deem the case moot or vacate merits determinations that still carry ongoing legal consequences.

John Roberts.reasoning: Article III counsels against resolving the INA’s merits on an essentially abstract record where the challenged “metering” policy has been rescinded and the government represents it has no concrete plan to reinstate it, raising advisory-opinion concerns and favoring a narrow disposition. Even if some aspects of the district court’s classwide declaration and the individual facilitation-of-entry order continue to operate, the proper course is to treat the controversy as at least substantially moot and vacate the lower-court judgment rather than issue a broad merits ruling about § 1225’s trigger point. Under the Court’s established mootness practice, when a case becomes moot in the course of review, vacatur is generally appropriate to prevent an unreviewable judgment from having continuing legal consequences (United States v. Munsingwear), and Acheson Hotels underscores the Court’s reluctance to adjudicate where the plaintiff’s claim no longer presents a live dispute. This approach preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves any future, concrete metering policy to be tested on a developed record, while avoiding an overbroad classwide injunction in a sensitive federal immigration context.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s text triggers the inspection regime for an "applicant for admission" who is "in the United States" and "arriving ... at a port of entry" or encountered after entry, 8 U.S.C. § 1225(a)(1), so DHS’s control over throughput and queueing outside that territorial trigger does not on its face violate § 1225’s mandatory inspection and referral provisions. Whatever limits Congress imposed on removal or asylum processing, courts should not expand them by treating presence just outside the sovereign line as equivalent to being "in the United States," particularly where immigration at the border implicates core political-branch authority. Even assuming some illegality in a particular practice, federal equitable power does not extend to classwide injunctions compelling executive processing or admission absent clear statutory authorization, and this Court has warned against remedies untethered to traditional equity and to the plaintiffs’ own injuries. Thuraissigiam confirms the limited nature of judicial intervention for would-be entrants at the threshold and counsels against judicially creating broad procedural entitlements or sweeping relief in this setting.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA provisions respondents invoke must be applied as written: § 1225(b) repeatedly turns on whether an applicant for admission is “in the United States” and “arriving … at a port of entry,” and DHS retains operational discretion over how many individuals it can safely and feasibly process at a given time rather than being judicially compelled to eliminate all queueing at the border line. Even assuming some statutory duties attach upon presentation, Congress in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(f)(1) sharply limits lower courts’ authority to “enjoin or restrain the operation” of Part IV (including § 1225) except “with respect to … an individual alien,” which precludes the kind of permanent classwide injunction entered here. Practical consequences confirm that reading: nationwide injunctions dictating port-of-entry throughput risk destabilizing border management and intruding on core Executive enforcement functions without unmistakable congressional authorization. At minimum, the broad classwide remedy cannot stand under § 1252(f)(1) and Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Comm.’s understanding of that provision as a limit on injunctive relief.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The INA’s mandatory text requires inspection of applicants “who are arriving in the United States” and who present “at a port of entry,” 8 U.S.C. § 1225(a)(1), and it separately guarantees the ability to seek asylum to those “physically present in the United States or … at a land border or port of entry,” 8 U.S.C. § 1158(a)(1); DHS cannot evade those duties by stopping people mere feet across the line to prevent the statutory trigger from attaching. Sale v. Haitian Centers Council confirms that Congress distinguished persons intercepted and kept “from reaching our shores” from those “arriv[ing] at the border,” 509 U.S. 155, 158, 160 (1993), underscoring that border-present asylum seekers fall within the statutory scheme, unlike high-seas interdiction. Given the acute, predictable harms metering imposes on vulnerable asylum seekers and the agency’s lack of authority to create a legal no-man’s-land at ports, equitable relief—including classwide relief where the practice operates categorically—is appropriate to remedy systemic unlawful conduct. The case is not moot because the injunction and declaration continue to bind the government as to the certified class and a named plaintiff’s facilitation order, so deciding the legality of the practice is not an advisory opinion under Article III.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Textually, § 1225(a)(1) applies to an applicant for admission who is "present in the United States" and is "arriv[ing]" at a port of entry; reading that phrase to allow DHS to stop people at (or just outside) the port so the mandatory inspection and fear-screening duties never attach would create an easily administrable loophole that defeats the statutory scheme Congress designed in §§ 1225 and 1158. The better reading—consistent with statutory coherence and workability—is that presentation for admission at the port (including being held just across an arbitrary line by U.S. officers as part of a throughput policy) triggers the inspection framework and access to asylum processing, rather than permitting evasion by moving the trigger point into Mexico. On justiciability, the case is not moot under ordinary voluntary-cessation principles because the injunction and declaratory judgment have continuing operative effect for the certified class and at least one named plaintiff, and Acheson Hotels v. Laufer underscores that mootness turns on whether the plaintiff has truly abandoned the controversy and whether effective relief remains—not merely on the government’s representation that it lacks “concrete plans” to resume the challenged policy. Any remedial concerns about breadth are best handled by tailoring relief, but the continuing obligations imposed by the existing judgment suffice to avoid an advisory opinion problem.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA repeatedly ties inspection and the attendant processing duties to an applicant who is “in the United States” and “who is an applicant for admission,” 8 U.S.C. § 1225(a)(1), and it is not this Court’s role to revise that territorial trigger to cover persons kept just outside the line by operational border measures. Reading §§ 1225 and 1158 to compel processing of individuals outside the United States risks an extraterritorial application Congress did not clearly prescribe and would press courts into managing day-to-day border throughput, raising separation-of-powers concerns. Even if some relief remains formally “live” because of an extant classwide declaration and an individualized facilitation order, the rescission of the challenged policy and the absence of concrete plans to reinstate it heighten Article III concerns against issuing what amounts to prospective advice about a policy not presently in force (cf. voluntary-cessation principles in Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw). Finally, to the extent ambiguity persists at the threshold of statutory coverage and the consequences include coercive judicial supervision of executive border operations, the better course is to adhere to the statute’s plain terms rather than extend them by implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Given the rescission of the challenged metering policy and the Government’s representation of no concrete plan to reinstate it, Article III’s prohibition on advisory opinions counsels against resolving the statutory merits in the abstract; under Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, the Court should be wary of continuing to adjudicate forward-looking relief when the underlying conduct has ceased and the case risks becoming moot. The remaining relief appears largely classwide and prospective, and federal courts should avoid broad structural injunctions in immigration administration absent a clearly ongoing, workably defined policy to enjoin. On the merits, the INA’s trigger language in 8 U.S.C. § 1225 (“in the United States” and “at a port of entry”) at least plausibly leaves DHS operational discretion to manage queues and throughput at ports without automatically initiating inspection duties for those not yet admitted into U.S. territory, and judicial restraint favors not expanding statutory mandates beyond their historically understood application. The proper course is to reverse the classwide injunction and, to the extent the case has become moot in relevant respects, vacate rather than issue a sweeping merits ruling untethered to a current policy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The statutory trigger in 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(1) is textually limited to an "applicant for admission" who is "arriving in the United States" (including one "who is brought to the United States"), and that language most naturally requires physical presence in the United States rather than mere arrival at the borderline or presence just outside a port of entry; reading "at a port of entry" to do all the work would strain the phrase "in the United States" and create the surplusage concern discussed at argument. Even if DHS’s operational control of port throughput is not unbounded, respondents’ theory would effectively let courts define the precise spatial trigger point for inspection in a way the text does not clearly command, especially in light of Congress’s detailed scheme for expedited removal and asylum screening in § 1225 and § 1158. Independently, Article III limits counsel against maintaining broad classwide prospective relief premised on a rescinded policy with no concrete plan to reinstate it; while an injunction directed to a named plaintiff may keep some controversy live, Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer underscores the need to ensure the Court is not opining in the abstract once the underlying dispute has evaporated. Given the ambiguity in the statutory trigger and the justiciability/relief problems, I would reverse the classwide merits holding and limit any remaining relief to concrete, non-advisory disputes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1225(a)(1) applies when an alien is “present in the United States” and “arrives … whether or not at a designated port of arrival,” and reading DHS’s inspection and fear-screening duties to turn on a manipulable physical line-drawing (so the government can stop people “just outside” a port to prevent statutory triggers) would permit evasion of Congress’s mandatory processing scheme in §§ 1225 and 1158. Given the district court’s continuing injunction requiring facilitation of entry for a named plaintiff and the judgment’s ongoing classwide effects, Article III is satisfied notwithstanding rescission of the formal policy; under Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, voluntary cessation and residual operative relief can keep a case live where concrete obligations remain. Practical consequences also counsel against a rule that incentivizes pushing enforcement into Mexico to avoid statutory constraints, undermining procedural fairness in asylum access. Federal courts therefore may enjoin metering on a classwide basis to remedy and prevent recurrence of ultra vires circumvention of the INA’s inspection/asylum-processing mandates.
